title: Multivalent supramolecular fluorescent probes for accurate disease imaging

predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: In Figures 2J and 2K, the x-axis intervals are visually equal, but the numerical increments between the tick marks are inconsistent, particularly for the last two values, which may mislead readers about the timing or progression of the data presented. The x-axis visual spacing does not correspond to the numerical scale.

The Results section reports the average hydrodynamic diameter (Dh) of Cy7.5AA@CDP as 459 nm (measured by DLS), while the Discussion/Summary section states the probes have an average hydrodynamic diameter of ~400 nm when explaining the renal clearance mechanism through tubular secretion. While this does not invalidate the paper's conclusions, these two reported values differ by approximately 60 nm (15% relative difference). Under lenient strictness this is noted but may represent rounding or context-dependent measurement.

summary: The paper 'Multivalent supramolecular fluorescent probes for accurate disease imaging' by Wu et al., published in Science Advances (DOI: 10.1126/sciadv.adp8719, 18 October 2024), was verified using exhaustive mode with lenient strictness. The paper's existence and core scientific claims were confirmed via web search. Two errors were detected: (1) A figure data integrity issue in Fig. 2J and 2K where x-axis visual intervals are equal but numerical increments are inconsistent (confidence: 0.85, erratum-worthy), and (2) A minor internal text-text inconsistency where the hydrodynamic diameter is reported as 459 nm in the Results but ~400 nm in the Discussion/Summary (confidence: 0.65, noted under lenient review). The binding stoichiometry calculations were mathematically verified as correct. The paper's statistical methodology uses n=3 biological replicates, which is standard for small-animal imaging studies. The paper makes substantial contributions to the field of optical imaging probe design and the errors detected do not undermine the core conclusions.
